Smooth constrained mortality forecasting (CP-splines)

Source: R/model-psplines.R
cp_splines.Rd

cp_splines() is the CP-spline model of Camarda (2019): the two-dimensional P-spline model of p_splines(), with coefficients of its own for the first year of life, whose forecast is constrained to age patterns and time trends like those of the fitting years. The code is written from the paper; the author's R code (supplementary material) was used to check details and results.

Usage

cp_splines(
  level_ageing = 0.95,
  level_change = 0.5,
  kappa = 10000,
  n_boot = 100,
  lambda = NULL,
  criterion = c("bic", "aic"),
  pord = 2,
  deg = 3,
  ndx = NULL,
  lambda_range = c(1e-04, 1e+06),
  infant = TRUE
)

Arguments

level_ageing, level_change

Levels of the central ranges of the rates of ageing and of change over the data years that bound the forecast (95% and 50% in Camarda 2019).

kappa

Weight of the asymmetric penalties, one value or one per constraint (ageing, change); 1e4 in Camarda (2019).

n_boot

Number of bootstrap samples (1000 in Camarda 2019). Each needs a forecast fit, so forecasts with many draws take time.

lambda

Smoothing parameters over age and years, c(age, year); NULL (default) selects them by criterion.

criterion

"bic" (default) or "aic".

pord

Order of the difference penalties, over age and years (one value for both).

deg

Degree of the B-splines, over age and years.

ndx

Numbers of intervals between knots over age and years; NULL gives about one knot per five years (see Details).

lambda_range

Search range of the smoothing parameters (the default of MortalitySmooth). A selected value at an end of the range gives a warning (class mt_warning_lambda_bound) when the criterion improves by more than 1 two decades beyond it.

infant

Give the first year of life its own coefficients (Camarda 2019, section 3.1).

Value

A model specification.

Details

The model has five steps (Camarda 2019, sections 3.1 to 3.2.2):

  1. A two-dimensional P-spline model is fitted to the data years (p_splines(), smoothing parameters by BIC). The first year of life gets a row of coefficients of its own, penalised over years but not connected over age with the following ages (section 3.1).

  2. At every age and data year, two derivatives of the fitted log rates are computed from the derivatives of the B-splines: over age, the rate of ageing, and over years, the rate of change (eq. 14-17).

  3. Bounds per age: the central range with level_ageing (default 95%) of the rates of ageing over the data years, and the central range with level_change (default 50%, the interquartile range) of the rates of change (empirical quantiles).

  4. The forecast fit (the basis over years extended over the forecast years with weight 0, as in p_splines()) adds asymmetric penalties: where a derivative in a forecast year lies outside its bounds, its squared distance to the bound is penalised with weight kappa (eq. 18-20). The cells outside their bounds are found again at every step of the scoring algorithm. Forecast age patterns thus keep the shape of the fitted ones, and the change of each age over time stays within the range of its past change.

  5. Uncertainty comes from a residual bootstrap (section 3.2.2). The deviance residuals of the fit of step 1 are resampled with replacement. With the observed deaths, each resampled residual gives bootstrap deaths: the value at which the observed deaths have that deviance residual (eq. 22). Steps 2 to 4 are repeated on every bootstrap sample, with the smoothing parameters, levels and kappa of the fit.

Each draw is the forecast of one bootstrap sample; the n_boot samples are used in turn when n_draws is larger. The draws thus carry the uncertainty of the fit only: the forecast has no innovations, and Camarda (2019) notes that the intervals are often narrower than those of other methods. Draws describe the expected rates; predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths, the observation model of the fit (the paper gives no method for prediction intervals of observed rates). With n_boot = 0 every draw is the forecast of the data.

The grid needs the first year of life as its own age group for step 1 to give it coefficients of its own (infant = TRUE and at least four age groups); otherwise all ages share the surface. Ages and missing cells are treated as in p_splines(). The bounds are ranges over the data years, so the model needs at least 10 of them.

Package-specific choices (reference unknown). As in p_splines(): cell ages, the knot spacing for age groups and the search of the smoothing parameters (the paper minimises the BIC; the author's code searches a grid over ranges set for its data). The knots lie on the range of the data without margins, as in the author's code. The basis over years of the forecast is that of the fit extended on the same knot spacing, as the paper describes, with the knots placed as in p_splines(); the author's code builds a new basis over the data and forecast years with one knot per five years (for French women, ages 0-100, 1950-2001, this changes the log rates forecast to 2021 by at most 0.001). The rate of ageing at age 0 is the difference of the log rates of the first two age groups divided by the distance between their cell ages (the author's code: single years of age). Cells without deaths have the deviance residual -sqrt(2 mu) (with 0 log 0 = 0), and their bootstrap deaths are r^2 / 2 for a negative resampled residual r and 0 for a positive one, the limit of eq. 22; the author's code gives these cells a residual drawn from the other cells. The scoring algorithm with asymmetric penalties stops when no coefficient changes by more than 1e-4 (relative to its size where that exceeds 1), after at most 100 steps, as in the author's code (relative changes).

References

Camarda CG (2019). Smooth constrained mortality forecasting. Demographic Research 41(38): 1091-1130. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2019.41.38

Currie ID, Durban M, Eilers PHC (2004). Smoothing and forecasting mortality rates. Statistical Modelling 4(4): 279-298. doi:10.1191/1471082X04st080oa

See also

p_splines() for the unconstrained forecast.

Examples

# \donttest{
x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2012)
fit <- mt_fit(cp_splines(n_boot = 20), x)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 10, n_draws = 20, seed = 1)
mt_parameters(fit)
